title: Artificial Sweeteners Linked to Faster Memory Decline, Major Study Finds
excerpt: An eight-year study of over 12,700 adults found that consuming common artificial sweeteners was associated with cognitive decline equivalent to 1.6 years of brain aging, particularly in people under 60.
body:
• A study published in Neurology found that people who consumed the most artificial sweeteners showed 62% faster cognitive decline than those who consumed the least
  • The effect was equivalent to about 1.6 years of extra brain aging and was most pronounced in adults under 60
  • Six of seven sweeteners studied — aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, and sorbitol — were linked to the decline; tagatose was not
  • The findings are observational and do not prove causation, but researchers urge a more critical look at sugar substitutes

The Study: Eight Years of Tracking

A study published in the journal Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, has found that higher consumption of common artificial sweeteners is associated with faster declines in memory and overall thinking skills over time.

Researchers at the University of São Paulo tracked 12,772 adults — average age 52, 55 percent women — over approximately eight years as part of the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Adult Health. Participants’ consumption of seven artificial sweeteners was estimated from food frequency questionnaires completed at the study’s start, and cognitive tests assessing verbal fluency, working memory, word recall, and processing speed were administered at the beginning, middle, and end of the study period.

Key Findings

After adjusting for factors including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, participants who consumed the highest amount of sweeteners showed cognitive decline that was 62 percent faster than those in the lowest consumption group. This translates to approximately 1.6 years of additional brain aging.

“Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar, however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time.”

— Prof. Claudia Kimie Suemoto, University of São Paulo

Those in the middle consumption group showed decline that was 35 percent faster, equivalent to about 1.3 years of aging. The highest-consumption group consumed an average of 191 milligrams of artificial sweeteners daily — roughly equivalent to one can of diet soda.

When researchers broke the results down by individual sweetener, six of the seven studied — aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, and sorbitol — were associated with faster decline in overall cognition, particularly memory. Tagatose was the only sweetener not linked to cognitive decline.

Age and Diabetes as Factors

One of the more surprising findings was that the association between sweetener consumption and cognitive decline appeared only in adults younger than 60. No significant link was found in participants over 60.

Dr. Andrew Budson, a lecturer in neurology at Harvard Medical School, described this result as “curious,” suggesting it likely reflects the difficulty of detecting small effects in older adults, whose rates of memory change vary widely, rather than evidence that sweeteners are harmless after 60.

The study also found that the link to faster cognitive decline was stronger in participants with diabetes than in those without — a notable finding given that people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes.

Limitations and Context

The study is observational and cannot establish that artificial sweeteners directly cause cognitive decline. Diet information was self-reported, introducing the possibility of recall errors. The research also could not fully account for all lifestyle factors that might influence both sweetener consumption and cognitive health.

The findings build on earlier work by the same Brazilian research group connecting ultraprocessed foods with faster cognitive decline. Many ultraprocessed foods marketed as sugar-free contain the artificial sweeteners studied in this research.

“More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup, or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives,” Suemoto said.

What This Means

The study does not suggest that people should immediately eliminate all artificial sweeteners, but it adds to a growing body of research questioning their assumed safety. Previous studies have linked artificial sweeteners to conditions including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and depression, but their potential impact on cognition had not been investigated at this scale.

For health-conscious consumers who have turned to diet sodas and sugar-free products as ostensibly healthier alternatives, the findings warrant a more careful assessment of daily intake, particularly during midlife.
